The nestling development of the Red-tailed black cockatoo (Calyptorhynchus banksii) begins with a relatively short incubation period. Eggs maintained under parental care at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] hatch after approximately 29 days [ab = approximately 29 days]. Upon emergence, the altricial neonate is notably small, with hatchlings recorded at a wet weight at birth of 25 grams [Wwb = 25 grams], reflecting the substantial energetic demands placed on the laying female. This initial mass is considerably lower than the ultimate wet weight of 738.6 grams [Wwi = 738.6 grams] attained by fully grown adults. The rapid growth phase from a downy chick to a feather-growing nestling is critical, and under the typical thermoneutral conditions for active individuals (41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]), the time since birth at fledging is recorded as 80 days [tx = 80 days]. This long nestling period is consistent with the life-history strategy of large, long-lived parrots, allowing for extensive feather maturation and muscle development before the critical first flight.

Following fledging, the young birds enter a prolonged period of nutritional dependence on their parents, which is typical for many Cacatuidae. Puberty, marking the onset of gonadal maturation, is reached at a relatively advanced age. Under standard thermoneutral conditions of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], the time since birth at puberty is 240 days [tp = 240 days]. This slow pace of sexual development is a reflection of the species’ extremely conservative reproductive strategy. Breeding does not commence immediately upon reaching sexual maturity, as individuals require additional time to acquire a territory and establish a pair bond. The first successful breeding event, or first brood, is typically deferred until a much later age. Under the same thermal conditions of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], the time since birth at first brood is 4 years [tR = 4 years], highlighting the significant pre-reproductive period.

The reproductive output of the Red-tailed black cockatoo is among the lowest recorded for any parrot species. Clutch size is strictly limited to a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch], and the interval between successive nesting attempts is protracted. Breeding females will typically produce a single clutch every 0.75 years [F_R_i = single clutch every 0.75 years], resulting in a remarkably low maximum reproductive rate. This strategy, a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch] repeated at a low frequency of one clutch every 0.75 years [F_R_i = one clutch every 0.75 years], is an adaptation to the unpredictable and often poor-quality food resources of their arid and semi-arid habitats, where each offspring requires an enormous parental investment to reach independence. The high investment in each chick is further evidenced by the substantial mass gain from the initial wet weight to the adult stage.

The lifespan of the Red-tailed black cockatoo is exceptionally long, a trait shared with many other members of the genus Calyptorhynchus. Field records and captive studies, conducted under a typical active body temperature regime of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 45.4 years [am = approximately 45.4 years]. This extended longevity is a cornerstone of the species’ life-history strategy, which prioritizes high adult survival over high fecundity. The slow pace of life, characterized by a late age at first reproduction and a low annual reproductive rate, is made viable only by the potential for many decades of breeding. This extreme longevity contrasts sharply with the much shorter lifespan of smaller passeriform birds, illustrating a classic slow-fast continuum within avian life histories.

Comparative physiological studies provide additional context for the life-history metrics of the Red-tailed black cockatoo. An important benchmark is the estimated initial wet weight of a newly laid egg, which is calculated at approximately 33.5 grams [Ww0 = approximately 33.5 grams]. This substantial egg mass, representing a significant portion of the female’s own body mass, is necessary to provision the large, slow-developing embryo. The mass of the egg at approximately 33.5 grams [Ww0 = approximately 33.5 grams] is consistent with the allometric scaling relationships observed for other large, long-lived psittacines. The high energetic cost of producing such a large egg, combined with the extended period of chick rearing, imposes a strict limit on the annual number of offspring a pair can successfully raise. This investment ensures that the single nestling, which grows from its modest 25 gram birth weight to its 738.6 gram adult mass, has the best possible chance of survival in a challenging environment.
